chapter_seo_title: Dao Gui Yi Xian Ch 293: Laughter, Coffins, and a Dying Man's Breakfast
chapter_meta_description: Li Huowang unleashes a devastating agony-link attack to break a siege, but as he lies dying, Gouwa haggles for his coffin and orders paper maids in one of the darkest comedic scenes yet.
og_title: Death Comes In Many Flavors: Tofu Pudding, Copper Coins, and Coffin Haggling
og_description: Li Huowang trades his own guts for a shared nightmare, then Gouwa negotiates funeral deals while the body’s still warm.
twitter_title: A hero falls. A merchant haggles. And someone orders a grand funeral.
twitter_description: Li Huowang’s agony-link breaks the siege—but Gouwa is already shopping for the best coffin deal and extra paper maids.

lore_anchors.definition: A self-sacrificial agony-magic technique that links the user's intense physical pain to all nearby beings, forcing them to share the same suffering.
A secret society named after a Daoist meditative concept, here perverted into a cult that weaponizes lies and confusion for amusement and power.
A grotesque, parasitic entity that can be used as a weapon or tool; its tentacles crawl into orifices and deliver horrifying payloads.
A Daoist ritual weapon composed of coins strung on red cord; it can both exorcise spirits and inflict physical wounds.
A minor character; sharp-faced, self-interested, and pragmatic, he handles logistics and funeral arrangements when others are incapacitated.
Paper effigy figures burned during funerals so the deceased has servants in the afterlife; a standard part of traditional Chinese burial rites.
In funeral context, a folk term for the eight bearers who carry the coffin; not to be confused with the Daoist immortals.
The ruling dynasty of the Dao-Twisted World; implied to be wealthy and relatively stable compared to surrounding regions.
The fifth and final segment of the traditional Chinese night-watch system, roughly 3–5 AM, just before dawn.
A classic Chinese breakfast dish; can be served sweet or savory. Here, Gouwa eats the sweet version with fried crullers.

cultural_notes_faq.a: The chapter suggests he is critically near death but not confirmed dead. His consciousness fades, and Bai Lingmiao is rushing toward him at the end of the open sequence. Gouwa’s funeral planning may be premature.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does Gouwa keep making funeral arrangements for dead shixiongs?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Gouwa’s line "I did it last time, too" reveals that his pragmatic role in the group is managing the aftermath of violence. He is not necessarily malicious—he is the one who handles the business of death when everyone else grieves.

cultural_notes_faq.q: What is the technique Li Huowang used on himself?
cultural_notes_faq.a: It’s called *Ripping Flesh and Pulling Bone*. It forces all nearby beings (friend or foe) to feel the same intense agony the user is experiencing. It’s a last-resort area-of-effect pain bomb with no friend-or-foe filter.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does the chapter pivot to Gouwa eating breakfast and haggling?
cultural_notes_faq.a: This contrast is deliberate. It shows that in the Dao-Twisted World, horror and bureaucracy coexist. While heroes lie dying, the mundane machinery of death—coffins, paper maids, and breakfast—keeps turning without sentimentality.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Is Gouwa a bad person for buying a coffin while his group leader is still alive?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Not necessarily. He is pragmatic, not malicious. His actions mirror the pervasive normalization of death in this world. He is preparing for what seems inevitable, not hoping for it.
